toyota_summary:
EU member states are pushing Brussels to give them wiggle room on green steel and cement quotas in the bloc's new industrial law. Several countries want the ability to adjust climate-friendly material requirements, arguing the rules are too rigid for domestic manufacturers. This matters because automakers rely heavily on steel and cement suppliers, and looser environmental standards could cheapen inputs but undercut the EU's competitive positioning on electric vehicles, where emissions-free production is supposed to be the selling point.

Germany's three largest automakers are losing ground in China and now facing the reverse problem at home: Chinese competitors are entering European markets with cheaper EVs and better battery technology. The German industry, which built its post-war recovery on Chinese growth, is no longer winning there. Watch whether the EU uses its industrial policy tools—subsidies, tariffs, or procurement rules—to shield European makers from Chinese competition over the next six months.

emails.subject_en: EU countries drop mandatory industrial acceleration areas from IAA
emails.summary_en: The EU Council's Irish presidency has softened the Industrial Accelerator Act, making industrial acceleration zones optional rather than mandatory for member states. For automakers, a key provision survives: manufacturers can self-declare EU-origin compliance if at least 85% of vehicles assembled the prior year met the rules, offering flexibility on local content requirements. The revised text also lets national governments retain more control over permitting, foreign investment screening, and approval of partner countries for origin equivalence.
emails.summary_ja: EU理事会のアイルランド議長国は「産業加速化法」を緩和し、加盟国に義務付けていた産業加速地域の指定を任意とする方向で調整している。自動車業界にとって重要な点として、前年に組み立てた車両の85%以上がEU原産規則を満たしていれば自己申告で対応できる柔軟措置が維持された。さらに改訂案では、許認可手続きや外国投資審査、原産地同等性を認めるパートナー国の承認について、加盟国政府の権限を強める内容となっている。

emails.subject_en: German automakers in freefall
emails.summary_en: Germany's top automakers—BMW, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz—posted sharply weaker first-half results as their once-lucrative China sales collapse, even as they hold steady in Europe and North America. Compounding the pain, Chinese EV makers are rapidly gaining ground in Europe, with their sales up 63% in the first half to nearly 10% of the EU market. The downturn lands just as Brussels negotiates the 2035 combustion-engine ban and new EU-preference rules, with industry lobbyists pushing hard to soften emissions targets.
emails.summary_ja: BMW、フォルクスワーゲン、メルセデス・ベンツなどドイツの主要自動車メーカーは、かつて稼ぎ頭だった中国市場での販売急減により、上半期決算が軒並み大幅に悪化した。欧州や北米では堅調を維持しているものの、それだけでは補いきれない状況だ。さらに追い打ちをかけるように、中国メーカーの欧州でのシェアが急拡大しており、上半期の販売台数は前年比63%増でEU市場の約1割を占めるまでになっている。この不振は、EUが2035年の内燃機関禁止や新たな「欧州優先」ルールを協議する時期と重なり、業界のロビイストは排出目標の緩和を強く求めている。

emails.subject_en: China made Germany’s car giants. Now it’s helping break them.
emails.summary_en: China's rapid advances in cheap, well-equipped electric vehicles are outpacing Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz, even as demand in China's overheated auto market shrank by a fifth this year. The result is billions in half-year losses, factory closures and thousands of job cuts across Germany, deepening the country's economic and political strain ahead of state elections. Executives warn the outlook is worsening, with Volkswagen's CEO citing unprecedented industry headwinds and rising risk.
